How to Find Property Records and Liens in Your County

Property records are split between several county offices. Learn which office holds ownership, tax, and lien information, how to search each one, and how to read what you find.

Key takeaways

  • ✓The assessor, recorder, and tax collector each hold different property information.
  • ✓A parcel number is the most reliable way to search.
  • ✓A free search is not a title search. Use a title company or attorney for a purchase.

Property records in the United States are kept at the county level, and no single national database covers them. The information you want is usually split between two or three offices, and each one answers a different question. Knowing which office to check saves hours of searching and keeps you from mistaking a tax-assessment page for a legal title record.

Which County Office Holds What

  • Assessor: estimates property value for taxation. It lists the owner of record, parcel number (APN), lot size, building details, and assessed value. It is not the authoritative record of who legally holds title.
  • Recorder, Register of Deeds, or Clerk of Court (the name varies by state): stores recorded deeds, mortgages or deeds of trust, easements, liens, and the releases that cancel them. This is the office that matters for ownership history and encumbrances.
  • Treasurer or Tax Collector: shows whether property taxes are paid, what is owed, and whether a tax lien or tax sale is pending.

Step 1: Gather Identifiers

Start with the full street address and, if you can get it, the parcel number. Parcel numbers are the most reliable way to search because addresses change and owner names can be misspelled or recorded in different forms. Most assessor websites let you look up the parcel number from an address, and that number can then be used at the recorder and tax collector.

Step 2: Check the Assessor Record

Open the county assessor's property search and enter the address or parcel number. Confirm the legal description, the owner name on the tax roll, the mailing address, and the assessed value. A mismatch between the owner on the tax roll and the person selling a property is worth investigating, since the roll can lag behind a recent sale by weeks or months.

Step 3: Search the Recorder's Index

Recorder databases are normally searched by grantor and grantee (seller and buyer), by document type, by date range, or by document number. To trace the history of a property, search the current owner as grantee to find the deed that gave them title, then search that deed's seller to move one step back. Look for each recorded mortgage and then look for the matching "release," "reconveyance," or "satisfaction of mortgage." A mortgage with no recorded release is not automatically still owed, since lenders sometimes record releases late, but it should be confirmed.

Common Types of Liens

  • Mortgage or deed of trust: secures a home loan.
  • Property tax lien: arises from unpaid local property taxes and typically ranks ahead of most other claims.
  • Mechanic's or contractor's lien: filed by a contractor or supplier who says they were not paid for work on the property.
  • HOA or condominium lien: filed by an association for unpaid assessments.
  • Judgment lien: created when a court judgment against an owner is recorded against their real estate.
  • Federal or state tax lien: a recorded notice that a tax agency claims the owner owes unpaid taxes.

Step 4: Check Taxes and Pending Actions

On the treasurer or tax collector site, look for delinquent amounts and any tax sale status. In the recorder's index, also search for a "lis pendens," which is a notice that a lawsuit or foreclosure involving the property has been filed. Court case records at the county clerk can show the lawsuit itself.

Costs, Limits, and Timing

  • Searching is free in many counties, but copies, and especially certified copies, usually carry a per-page fee.
  • Online indexes may only reach back a certain number of years. Older deeds can require a visit, a records request, or microfilm.
  • Recording is not instant. A deed or lien filed this week may take days or weeks to appear in the online index.
  • Search every spelling and name variation for the owner, including maiden names, initials, and entity names, because indexing errors are common.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating assessed value as market value or as proof of ownership.
  • Searching only the owner's name and missing liens recorded against the property description or parcel.
  • Ignoring recorded releases and wrongly assuming an old lien is still active.
  • Relying on a free online search as a substitute for a title search before a purchase.

When a Free Search Is Not Enough

Public searches are a good way to screen a property or confirm facts, but they are not a title guarantee. For a purchase, a refinance, or a lien dispute, title companies and real estate attorneys search the full chain of title and offer title insurance, which protects you if something is missed. Procedures and office names differ by state, so confirm details with the county office directly.
